summary: An experimental document that compares the functionality of LPD and IPP and helps with building gateways between the two protocols. It is part of the set of documents describing IPP.

eli5.summary: An old way of sending print jobs and a new way do similar things. This explains how to translate between them.

questions: what is the difference between lpd and ipp
how to map lpd commands to ipp operations
what is an lpd to ipp mapper
which lpd functions have no ipp equivalent
subtitle: How a gateway can translate between the old Line Printer Daemon protocol and the Internet Printing Protocol.

tldr.problem: Many print systems spoke the Line Printer Daemon (LPD) protocol, while the new Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) had a different model. Implementers of gateways between the two needed a shared understanding of how the pieces correspond.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps each LPD command, sub-command and control file line to an IPP operation or attribute, and each IPP operation back to LPD commands, calling the translating gateway a mapper. It also fixes the text layout of the LPD queue-status replies.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental, non-standards-track document that records what could and could not be mapped, and lists LPD functions that have no IPP equivalent.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Experimental, not on the standards track

today: RFC 2569 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says it is not on the standards track and that its IESG note expected a standards-track IPP version to differ from the one it maps.

sections.title: Why a Mapping Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 2569 is one of the documents describing the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) version 1.0. It gives advice to implementers of gateways between IPP and the Line Printer Daemon (LPD) protocol of RFC 1179, and compares the functionality of the two protocols.

RFC 1179 was written in 1990 to document existing LPD implementations, and vendors have since added undocumented extensions, all of them extra control file commands. This RFC does not address those extensions, nor the obsolete control file functions meant for text-only formats. It maps current practice only, and says where practice deviates from RFC 1179.

The mapping runs in both directions. The LPD-to-IPP mapper accepts LPD and speaks IPP; the IPP-to-LPD mapper does the reverse. The RFC says it is an informational document that is not on the standards track, and that it also serves as an example giving more insight into IPP.
sections.eli5: Some printers speak an old language and some speak a new one. This document explains how a translator in the middle can let them talk to each other.

sections.title: From LPD Commands to IPP Operations
sections.content:
The LPD-to-IPP mapper turns each LPD command into IPP operations. print-any-waiting-jobs is simply ignored, because an IPP printer handles waiting jobs without such a nudge. remove-jobs becomes one Cancel-Job for each job referenced, and both queue-state commands become Get-Printer-Attributes plus Get-Jobs.

receive-a-printer-job becomes either Print-Job (one data file) or Create-Job followed by one Send-Document per data file. With several data files the mapper SHALL use Create-Job if the printer supports it. If the printer lacks Create-Job and Send-Document, each data file becomes a separate Print-Job, turning one LPD job into several IPP jobs. The mapper MUST send Create-Job first, even when the LPD control file arrives after the data files.

The LPD control file sub-command is roughly equivalent to Create-Job and the data file sub-command to Send-Document. The mapper SHALL reject a data file whose byte count is 0, since no implementation supports the unspecified-length feature RFC 1179 alludes to. An abort sub-command, or a dropped connection, cancels the job in progress, either by closing the IPP connection or by calling Cancel-Job.

For remove-jobs, the mapper SHALL NOT use the agent name root when end users cancel their own jobs. Doing so is a potential security violation and could make the printer's notification mislead a user about who cancelled the job.
sections.eli5: Each thing the old language can ask for has a matching request in the new language. A few requests, like a nudge to start printing, are not needed at all, so the translator just skips them.

sections.title: Queue Status Replies and Control File Lines
sections.content:
RFC 1179 does not say what a queue-state reply looks like, so this RFC requires the mapper to follow existing practice. The short form is a printer-status line, a heading line (Rank, Owner, Job, Files, Total Size) and one line per job. An empty queue is reported as no entries. The long form puts each job in a block with a description line and one line per file, adding the host and copies fields. Appendices A and B give ABNF for both.

Fields come from IPP attributes: rank from number-of-intervening-jobs (preferred over list position because a printer may omit secret jobs), job from job-id, files from document-name (a comma-separated list truncated to the first 24 characters), and total size from job-k-octets multiplied by 1024 and by copies.

LPD control file lines also map to attributes. H (host) and P (user) are required in every job. P becomes requesting-user-name, and the mapper always sets ipp-attribute-fidelity to true so it need not learn which attributes a printer supports. J maps to job-name, and L to job-sheets. The document functions f and l map to the document format application/octet-stream, o to application/PostScript, and N to document-name. The number of copies is found by counting how many times a data file is named.

The RFC notes that LPD's M (mail when printed) has no IPP notification mechanism, so a gateway would have to poll with Get-Job-Attributes. LPD text operands are limited to 31 or 99 characters, while IPP values allow 255 or 1023 octets, so nothing is lost in the LPD-to-IPP direction.
sections.eli5: The old language reports the line at the printer as a little table, and the translator has to fill in each box from what the new language says. Small notes on the job, like who sent it and how many copies, get translated one by one.

sections.title: From IPP Operations to LPD Commands
sections.content:
The IPP-to-LPD mapper turns Print-Job, Print-URI and the Create-Job family into the LPD receive-a-printer-job command followed by print-any-waiting-jobs. Cancel-Job becomes remove-jobs, and the three read operations become a short or long queue-state request. Validate-Job is done by the mapper itself, since LPD supports so few attributes that there is little to check.

The control file is built from the IPP attributes, with the functions in a fixed order: H then P, then optional ones, then f, U and N for each document, with f repeated once per copy. A mapper SHALL send its own host, because some LPD systems require it to match the host that sends remove-jobs, and it SHALL NOT send the o function.

Because some print systems start printing when the control file arrives and others when the first data file arrives, the RFC recommends that the order of control file and data files be configurable. For Create-Job, the control file is sent only after the last Send-Document or Send-URI, since it carries all the document names and formats.

LPD limits what can be reported back. Get-Printer-Attributes supports at most printer-state and printer-state-reasons, and Get-Job-Attributes at most six job attributes such as job-id, copies and job-k-octets. The mapper SHALL reject a job that uses unsupported attributes unless fidelity is best-effort. Error code conversion is not addressed.
sections.eli5: Going the other way, the translator packs the new language's request into the old language's envelope, in the exact order the old printer expects. It can only tell you a few things back, because the old language does not report much.

sections.title: Security and Unsupported Functions
sections.content:
The RFC says there are no security issues beyond those already covered in the IPP encoding and transport document (RFC 2565), the IPP model document (RFC 2566) and the LPD document (RFC 1179). An IESG note adds that the expected standards-track IPP would add strong authentication and privacy features and an ipp: URL type supporting them, and encourages experiments with Transport Layer Security.

Appendix C lists LPD functions with no IPP equivalent, such as C (class for banner page), I (indent printing), W (width of output) and the troff font functions. The LPD-to-IPP mapper ignores these. Other lower-case functions name document formats with no IPP equivalent, including d (DVI), t (troff) and v (raster); the LPD-to-IPP mapper rejects jobs that request them unless someone registers the format.
sections.eli5: The translator adds no new danger beyond what the two languages already carry. Some old-language words have no new-language match, so the translator skips them or refuses the job.
